newsitem.title: QATAR: Qatar's to vote in municipal poll next year.
newsitem.headline: Qatar's to vote in municipal poll next year.

text.p: All Qataris -- including women -- above age 18 will be allowed to vote in the country's first-ever municipal elections expected early next year according to a new draft law, a Qatari minister said on Wednesday.

"A draft law organising municipalities and the elections is ready and it will be submitted soon to the cabinet and advisory council for discussion and approval," said the Minister of Justice Najeeb Mohammad al-Nuaimi.
The minister said the minimum age for candidates would be 25. "A proposal is also being discussed to allow women also to contest the elections," he said.
"Army and police personnel will, however, not be allowed to participate in the vote," al-Nuaimi added.
The total number of seats to be filled at the Central Municipal Council will be 21, according to the draft law.

"The Emir wanted all members to be elected. But after several discussions and going by the experience of other states it was proposed that one-fourth of the council members be nominated," al-Nuaimi said.

The elections plan was announced by Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani, 47, as a first step towards enlisting public support and developing grassroots democracy in his tiny Gulf Arab state. Sheikh Hamad ousted his father, Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad al-Thani, 65, in a bloodless coup in June 1995.
Qatar, with a native population of around 160,000 and a total population of 650,000 including expatriate workers, is the first state in the Gulf region to order municipal elections.

Kuwait has the only elected parliament in the region, but only men can vote. Neighbouring Bahrain experimented with an elected legislature in the early 70s but the emir dissolved it in 1975, provoking public unrest.

Al-Nuaimi said Qatar's election was also "experimental". The tenure of the elected council would be for three years and during this period the advantages and disadvantages of running the country through elections would be examined, he said.
